name: Edit a live Deployment in place
objective: CKAD › Application Deployment. Drill EVERY way to change a Deployment that already exists — WITHOUT deleting it: scale, rolling image update, rollback, set resources, inject config, change strategy, targeted JSON patch, and rollout restart. Graded exactly, per requirement.

questions.title: Set resources in place
questions.teach:
`kubectl set resources deployment/<name> --requests=cpu=100m,memory=128Mi --limits=cpu=200m,memory=256Mi` edits requests/limits on a live template in place (triggering a rollout) — no hand-editing YAML.

**Gotcha:** units are exact — `100m` cpu, `128Mi` memory; a typo or wrong unit fails the match.
questions.prompt:
On Deployment `cache` in `deploy-learn`, set container resources **in place**: requests `cpu=100m, memory=128Mi`; limits `cpu=200m, memory=256Mi`.

Target: `cache`'s container has exactly those requests and limits.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n deploy-learn set resources deployment/cache --requests=cpu=100m,memory=128Mi --limits=cpu=200m,memory=256Mi
kubectl -n deploy-learn get deploy cache -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources}'
questions.eli5:
Imagine a Deployment is a recipe card taped to the fridge, and the kitchen keeps cooking copies of whatever that card says. You don't throw the card away to change the meal — you just edit the card, and the kitchen re-cooks.

Here, the edit is about **portions**:

- A **request** is "please reserve me at least this much counter space to start cooking" — the kitchen won't seat your pod on a node unless that much is free.
- A **limit** is "never let me grab more than this" — a hard ceiling. Go over the memory ceiling and you get kicked out (killed).

`kubectl set resources` is a sticky-note edit: it changes the portion sizes right on the live recipe card. Because the card (the pod template) changed, the kitchen quietly re-cooks the dishes with the new portions — that's a rollout, no deleting required.

Two measuring units matter: CPU is counted in **millicores** where `1000m = 1 whole CPU` (so `100m` is a tenth of a CPU), and memory in **Mi/Gi** (`128Mi` is 128 mebibytes).

**Watch out for:**

- **Units must be exact.** `100m` cpu and `128Mi` memory — a typo like `128M`, `128mi`, or `100` (no `m`) changes the meaning or fails the match.
- **Setting resources triggers a rollout** because it edits the pod template — the pods restart with the new values.
- **Memory limit is a hard kill (OOMKilled); CPU limit only throttles** — it won't kill the pod, just slow it.
- A **request** affects *scheduling*; a **limit** affects *runtime enforcement* — they are not the same knob.
questions.deepDive:
## Set resources in place — full rundown

### Mental model
A Deployment owns a **pod template** (`.spec.template`). Change anything inside that template and the Deployment controller rolls a new ReplicaSet. `kubectl set resources` is an imperative one-liner that patches the template's container `resources` block — no YAML editing, no delete/recreate — and the edit **triggers a rolling update**.

- **requests** → used by the scheduler to decide if a pod *fits* a node (reservation).
- **limits** → enforced at runtime by the kubelet/cgroups (ceiling).

### The command
```bash
kubectl set resources deployment/<name> \
  --requests=cpu=100m,memory=128Mi \
  --limits=cpu=200m,memory=256Mi
```
Scope it to a container with `-c <container>` (default: all containers). Target init containers with `--limits ... --containers='*'` style flags only via `-c`.

### Flags
| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--requests` | sets `resources.requests` (cpu/memory/ephemeral-storage) |
| `--limits` | sets `resources.limits` |
| `-c, --containers` | glob of container names to patch (default `*`) |
| `--dry-run=client -o yaml` | preview the patched template |
| `--local` | edit a local file, don't hit the API |

### Units — get these exactly right
| Resource | Unit | Examples | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| CPU | millicores | `100m` = 0.1 CPU, `1` = `1000m` = 1 CPU | `m` = milli; bare number = whole cores |
| Memory | bytes w/ suffix | `128Mi`, `256Mi`, `1Gi` | `Mi`/`Gi` are power-of-two (binary); `M`/`G` are decimal — **not** interchangeable |

```yaml
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 128Mi
  limits:
    cpu: 200m
    memory: 256Mi
```

### Verify
```bash
kubectl get deploy <name> \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources}'; echo
kubectl rollout status deployment/<name>
```

### Requests vs limits behaviour
| Aspect | request | limit |
|---|---|---|
| Who uses it | scheduler (placement) | kubelet / cgroups (runtime) |
| Over CPU | N/A (guaranteed share) | **throttled**, never killed |
| Over memory | N/A | **OOMKilled** |
| Missing | pod can be scheduled anywhere | no ceiling (can starve node) |

### QoS as a side effect
The requests/limits combo sets the pod's **QoS class**:
- `requests == limits` for every resource → **Guaranteed**
- some requests/limits set → **Burstable**
- none set → **BestEffort** (first to be evicted under pressure)

Here `100m/128Mi` request vs `200m/256Mi` limit → **Burstable**.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`set resources` triggers a rollout** — the template changed. If the grader checks "didn't delete it", that's fine; pods restart but the Deployment object persists.
- **`Mi` ≠ `M`.** `128Mi` = 134,217,728 bytes; `128M` = 128,000,000 bytes. Graders usually want the `Mi` form.
- **Bare CPU number means whole cores.** `--requests=cpu=100` asks for 100 CPUs (will stay Pending), not `100m`.
- Patching all containers unintentionally: add `-c <name>` when a pod has sidecars.
- A **LimitRange** in the namespace can inject defaults or reject your values — if a set fails, check `kubectl get limitrange`.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n deploy-learn set resources deployment/cache \
  --requests=cpu=100m,memory=128Mi \
  --limits=cpu=200m,memory=256Mi
kubectl -n deploy-learn get deploy cache \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources}'; echo
```

questions.title: Inject config from a ConfigMap
questions.teach:
`kubectl set env deployment/<name> --from=configmap/<cm>` injects one env var **per key** of the ConfigMap in place (each wired as a `configMapKeyRef`). Verify with `kubectl set env deployment/<name> --list`.

**Gotcha:** `--from` adds individual `configMapKeyRef` vars, not a bulk `envFrom` block — the keys appear as named env vars.
questions.prompt:
ConfigMap `worker-cfg` (keys `LOG_LEVEL`, `REGION`) exists in `deploy-learn`. Inject **all its keys** as environment variables into the `worker` Deployment, in place, using `kubectl set env --from`.

Target: `worker`'s container has env `LOG_LEVEL` and `REGION`, each sourced from ConfigMap `worker-cfg`.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n deploy-learn set env deployment/worker --from=configmap/worker-cfg`, then `kubectl -n deploy-learn set env deployment/worker --list`.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n deploy-learn set env deployment/worker --from=configmap/worker-cfg
kubectl -n deploy-learn set env deployment/worker --list

verification.description: worker env LOG_LEVEL + REGION sourced from ConfigMap worker-cfg

questions.eli5:
A **ConfigMap** is a little box of labelled settings — like a jar of sticky notes, each note having a name (`LOG_LEVEL`) and a value (`debug`). Your app reads these as **environment variables**: named settings it can look up while running.

`kubectl set env deployment/worker --from=configmap/worker-cfg` walks into that jar, takes **every** note, and pins each one onto your app's recipe card as its own env var. A jar with keys `LOG_LEVEL` and `REGION` gives you two env vars, `LOG_LEVEL` and `REGION`, each one still *pointing back* to the jar (a `configMapKeyRef`) rather than copying the value in flat.

Why point back instead of copy? So the wiring is traceable — you can see the var came from `worker-cfg`.

To check your work, ask the recipe card to read its env list back: `kubectl set env deployment/worker --list`.

**Watch out for:**

- **`--from` creates one env var *per key*, each as a `configMapKeyRef`** — it does **not** add a single bulk `envFrom` block. If the grader wants individually-named keyRef vars, this is the right tool; if it wanted `envFrom`, that's a different thing.
- **The keys become the env var names exactly** — `LOG_LEVEL` stays `LOG_LEVEL`. Add `--prefix=` if you need to rename them.
- **Editing env is a template change, so it triggers a rollout** — pods restart.
- **The ConfigMap must already exist** in the same namespace, or the pods will fail to start (CreateContainerConfigError) because the keyRef can't resolve.
- Changing the ConfigMap later does **not** auto-update env vars in running pods — you'd need a `rollout restart`.
questions.deepDive:
## Inject ConfigMap keys as env — full rundown

### Mental model
There are two ways a ConfigMap becomes env vars, and they produce **different YAML**:

| Approach | kubectl | Produces | Var names |
|---|---|---|---|
| Per-key keyRef | `set env --from=configmap/cm` | one `env[]` entry **per key**, each a `configMapKeyRef` | the ConfigMap keys |
| Bulk import | (YAML) `envFrom: [{configMapRef: {name: cm}}]` | a single `envFrom` block | the ConfigMap keys (optionally prefixed) |

`kubectl set env --from` does the **first** one. This drills that distinction — a classic exam trap.

### The command
```bash
kubectl set env deployment/worker --from=configmap/worker-cfg
```
Resulting template (one entry per key):
```yaml
env:
- name: LOG_LEVEL
  valueFrom:
    configMapKeyRef:
      name: worker-cfg
      key: LOG_LEVEL
- name: REGION
  valueFrom:
    configMapKeyRef:
      name: worker-cfg
      key: REGION
```

### Useful flags
| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--from=configmap/<cm>` | import every key as a keyRef var |
| `--from=secret/<s>` | same, from a Secret (`secretKeyRef`) |
| `--prefix=APP_` | prepend a prefix to each generated var name |
| `--keys=LOG_LEVEL` | import only specific keys from the source |
| `-e NAME=value` | set a literal env var |
| `-e NAME-` | **remove** an env var (trailing dash) |
| `--list` | print current env (and `valueFrom` refs) without changing anything |
| `--containers/-c` | which container(s) to patch |

### Verify
```bash
kubectl set env deployment/worker --list
kubectl get deploy worker \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].env}' | jq .
```

### set env --from vs envFrom
```yaml
# envFrom = bulk, ONE block, no per-key entries
envFrom:
- configMapRef:
    name: worker-cfg
```
- `envFrom` pulls **all current and future keys** at container start as a block; keys with invalid env names are silently skipped.
- `set env --from` snapshots the **current** keys into explicit `env` entries. New keys added later are **not** picked up until you re-run it.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`--from` ≠ `envFrom`.** If the task says "use envFrom", `set env --from` is the wrong answer — you must hand-write the `envFrom` block.
- **Editing env triggers a rollout** (template change) — pods restart.
- **ConfigMap must exist in the same namespace first**, or pods hit `CreateContainerConfigError` because the keyRef can't resolve.
- **Live ConfigMap edits don't propagate to env-sourced vars** in running pods — unlike mounted volumes. You need `kubectl rollout restart` to pick up changes.
- Keys that aren't valid env var names (e.g. contain `-` or `.`) cause issues — valid names match `[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*`.
- `--list` is read-only — great for verification, changes nothing.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n deploy-learn set env deployment/worker --from=configmap/worker-cfg
kubectl -n deploy-learn set env deployment/worker --list
```

questions.title: Change the update strategy
questions.teach:
`.spec.strategy.type` controls how pods are replaced on a template change. `Recreate` kills all old pods then creates new ones (brief downtime, never two versions at once); patch it in place with `kubectl patch deployment <name> -p '{"spec":{"strategy":{"type":"Recreate","rollingUpdate":null}}}'`.

**Gotcha:** `Recreate` must **not** carry a `rollingUpdate` block — set it `null` or the API rejects the change.
questions.prompt:
Change Deployment `cache`'s update strategy to **Recreate**, in place.

Target: `cache`'s `.spec.strategy.type` is `Recreate`.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n deploy-learn patch deployment cache -p '{"spec":{"strategy":{"type":"Recreate","rollingUpdate":null}}}'
kubectl -n deploy-learn get deploy cache -o jsonpath='{.spec.strategy.type}'
questions.eli5:
When a Deployment needs to swap its pods for new ones (say you changed the image), the **strategy** is *how* it does the swap. There are two styles, like repainting a row of shops:

- **RollingUpdate** (the default): repaint one shop at a time. While shop 3 is closed for paint, shops 1, 2, 4, 5 stay open — customers are never fully locked out. But for a moment you have *both* freshly-painted and old shops running side by side.
- **Recreate**: close **all** the shops at once, repaint everything, then reopen them all new. There's a gap where nothing is open (downtime) — but you never have old and new mixed together at the same time.

You'd choose **Recreate** when two versions must never run at once — for example an app whose old and new versions can't share the same database schema.

`kubectl patch` edits this setting right on the live Deployment, no delete needed.

**Watch out for:**

- **Recreate causes brief downtime** — every pod goes down before new ones come up. Never pick it for something that must stay available.
- **A `Recreate` strategy must NOT carry a `rollingUpdate` block.** The two settings are mutually exclusive. When switching to Recreate you must set `rollingUpdate` to `null` in the same patch, or the API rejects it.
- The upside of Recreate: **never two versions live at once** — the reason you'd ever choose it.
- Switching strategy changes *future* rollouts; it doesn't restart pods by itself.
questions.deepDive:
## Change the update strategy — full rundown

### Mental model
`.spec.strategy` tells the Deployment controller **how to replace pods** when the pod template changes. Two types:

| Type | How it swaps | Downtime | Two versions at once? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **RollingUpdate** (default) | gradually: scale new RS up, old RS down | none (if tuned) | **yes**, transiently |
| **Recreate** | kill all old pods, then create all new | **yes** | **no**, never |

Choose `Recreate` when old+new must not coexist (e.g. incompatible DB migrations, exclusive locks, singleton workloads).

### The in-place patch
```bash
kubectl patch deployment <name> \
  -p '{"spec":{"strategy":{"type":"Recreate","rollingUpdate":null}}}'
```
The default patch type is a **strategic merge patch**. Setting `rollingUpdate:null` deletes the sub-object.

### Why rollingUpdate must be nulled
The API validation forbids a `rollingUpdate` block when `type: Recreate`. If you only change the type, the old `rollingUpdate` (`maxSurge`/`maxUnavailable`) lingers and the update is rejected:
```
The Deployment "cache" is invalid: spec.strategy.rollingUpdate:
Forbidden: may not be specified when strategy `type` is 'Recreate'
```
Setting it `null` in the same patch clears it atomically.

### RollingUpdate knobs (for contrast)
```yaml
spec:
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 25%          # extra pods allowed above desired during roll
      maxUnavailable: 25%    # pods allowed to be down during roll
```
| Field | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `maxSurge` | 25% | how many **extra** pods above `replicas` may exist mid-roll |
| `maxUnavailable` | 25% | how many pods may be **unavailable** mid-roll |

Both accept a count or percentage. They cannot **both** be 0.

### Verify
```bash
kubectl get deploy <name> -o jsonpath='{.spec.strategy.type}'; echo
kubectl get deploy <name> -o jsonpath='{.spec.strategy}'; echo
```

### Equivalent approaches
```bash
# strategic merge (shown above) — simplest
kubectl patch deployment cache -p '{"spec":{"strategy":{"type":"Recreate","rollingUpdate":null}}}'

# JSON patch — must remove rollingUpdate explicitly
kubectl patch deployment cache --type=json \
  -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/strategy/type","value":"Recreate"},
       {"op":"remove","path":"/spec/strategy/rollingUpdate"}]'

# kubectl edit — interactive (delete the rollingUpdate lines by hand)
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`Recreate` + leftover `rollingUpdate` = rejected.** Always null/remove it when switching to Recreate.
- **Switching strategy does not restart pods** by itself — it only affects the *next* template change.
- A JSON-patch `remove` on a non-existent `/spec/strategy/rollingUpdate` **errors**; strategic-merge `null` is safe whether or not it exists.
- `Recreate` means a real **availability gap** — never use it for always-on services.
- `maxSurge`+`maxUnavailable` both 0 is invalid for RollingUpdate.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n deploy-learn patch deployment cache \
  -p '{"spec":{"strategy":{"type":"Recreate","rollingUpdate":null}}}'
kubectl -n deploy-learn get deploy cache -o jsonpath='{.spec.strategy.type}'; echo
```

questions.title: Targeted change with a JSON patch
questions.teach:
A **JSON patch** (`kubectl patch --type=json`, RFC 6902) is op-based (`add`/`replace`/`remove`) targeting an exact **path** — the scalpel for one field or list index: `--type=json -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/imagePullPolicy","value":"IfNotPresent"}]'`.

**Gotcha:** paths are 0-indexed and must already exist — use `op: add` if the field isn't set yet, or `replace` fails.
questions.prompt:
Using a **JSON patch** (`kubectl patch --type=json`), set the `imagePullPolicy` of the container in Deployment `frontend` to `IfNotPresent`, in place.

Target: `frontend`'s container `imagePullPolicy` is `IfNotPresent`.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n deploy-learn patch deployment frontend --type=json -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/imagePullPolicy","value":"IfNotPresent"}]'` (use `add` instead of `replace` if the field isn't set yet).
questions.solution:
kubectl -n deploy-learn patch deployment frontend --type=json -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/imagePullPolicy","value":"IfNotPresent"}]'
kubectl -n deploy-learn get deploy frontend -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].imagePullPolicy}'

verification.description: frontend container imagePullPolicy == IfNotPresent (via JSON patch)

questions.eli5:
There are a few ways to edit a live object, and they're like different editing tools for a document.

- A **strategic merge patch** (the default `kubectl patch`) is like saying "here's the new value for this setting" and Kubernetes figures out how to merge it in nicely.
- A **JSON patch** (`--type=json`) is the **scalpel**: a precise list of operations, each aimed at one exact spot by its **path**. You say `replace the value at this address with that`, like giving GPS coordinates to a single field.

The address uses slashes, and **lists are numbered from 0**. So `/spec/template/spec/containers/0/imagePullPolicy` means: the Deployment's pod template → its first container (number 0) → that container's `imagePullPolicy` field.

`imagePullPolicy` just controls when the node bothers to download the image: `IfNotPresent` means "only pull if I don't already have it locally."

Each op has a verb: **`replace`** (change something that's already there), **`add`** (create it if it's missing, or insert into a list), **`remove`** (delete it).

**Watch out for:**

- **Paths are 0-indexed.** The first container is `/.../containers/0`, not `/1`.
- **`replace` fails if the field doesn't exist yet.** If `imagePullPolicy` was never set, use `add` instead — `add` both creates and overwrites.
- **The patch is a JSON *array*** of ops — note the square brackets `[ { ... } ]`, even for a single op.
- **The parent path must exist.** You can `add` a leaf, but you can't `add` deep into a parent that isn't there.
- Mind shell quoting: wrap the `-p='[...]'` so your shell doesn't mangle the JSON.
questions.deepDive:
## Targeted change with a JSON patch — full rundown

### Mental model
`kubectl patch` supports three patch types. A **JSON patch** (RFC 6902) is op-based and path-precise — the scalpel for one field or one list element.

| `--type` | Format | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| `strategic` (default) | partial object, K8s-aware merge of lists | most everyday edits |
| `merge` (RFC 7386) | partial object, dumb replace of lists | simple scalar/map edits |
| `json` (RFC 6902) | array of `{op, path, value}` ops | exact field / list-index surgery |

### The command
```bash
kubectl patch deployment frontend --type=json \
  -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/imagePullPolicy","value":"IfNotPresent"}]'
```

### JSON Pointer paths (RFC 6901)
- `/`-separated, **lists are 0-indexed**: `/spec/template/spec/containers/0`.
- `-` means "end of array" for `add`: `.../containers/0/env/-` appends.
- Keys containing `/` or `~` are escaped `~1` and `~0` respectively.

### The ops
| op | Behaviour | Fails when… |
|---|---|---|
| `add` | set a field (create or overwrite); into a list = insert at index | parent path missing |
| `replace` | overwrite an **existing** value | target path does **not** exist |
| `remove` | delete a field or list element | target path missing |
| `copy` | copy value from `from` to `path` | source missing |
| `move` | move value from `from` to `path` | source missing |
| `test` | assert `path` equals `value` (no-op if true) | value mismatch → whole patch fails |

```json
[
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/imagePullPolicy","value":"IfNotPresent"},
  {"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/env/-","value":{"name":"X","value":"y"}},
  {"op":"remove","path":"/spec/replicas"}
]
```

### imagePullPolicy values (the field being set)
| Value | Behaviour | Default when… |
|---|---|---|
| `IfNotPresent` | pull only if image absent on node | tag is a fixed version (e.g. `:1.26`) |
| `Always` | pull on every pod start | tag is `:latest` or omitted |
| `Never` | never pull; must be pre-loaded | — |

### Verify
```bash
kubectl get deploy frontend \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].imagePullPolicy}'; echo
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`replace` on a missing field errors** (`the server rejected ... Unable to find`). Use `add` when the field may be unset — `add` creates *or* overwrites.
- **Paths are 0-indexed** — first container is `/0`.
- **The `-p` value is a JSON array**, always wrapped in `[ ... ]`, even for one op.
- **Parent must exist.** `add` creates a leaf or array element, not a whole missing ancestor chain.
- **Strategic vs JSON for lists:** strategic merge merges list items by key (e.g. container `name`); JSON patch addresses them by numeric index. Picking the wrong type silently edits the wrong thing.
- Quote carefully: `-p='[...]'` in single quotes keeps the shell out of your JSON.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n deploy-learn patch deployment frontend --type=json \
  -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/imagePullPolicy","value":"IfNotPresent"}]'
kubectl -n deploy-learn get deploy frontend \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].imagePullPolicy}'; echo
```

questions.title: Reload config with rollout restart
questions.teach:
`kubectl rollout restart deployment/<name>` rolls the pods with no real spec change — it stamps a `kubectl.kubernetes.io/restartedAt` timestamp annotation on the template, triggering a fresh rollout. This is the clean way to pick up a changed ConfigMap/Secret used via env.

**Gotcha:** restart ≠ delete — the controller rolls new pods in gracefully rather than killing everything at once.
questions.prompt:
Roll the `worker` Deployment's pods in place (no spec change) so they'd pick up a changed ConfigMap — using `rollout restart`.

Target: `worker`'s pod template carries the `kubectl.kubernetes.io/restartedAt` annotation.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n deploy-learn rollout restart deployment/worker`, then `kubectl -n deploy-learn rollout status deployment/worker`.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n deploy-learn rollout restart deployment/worker
kubectl -n deploy-learn rollout status deployment/worker

verification.description: worker rolled via rollout restart (restartedAt annotation present)

questions.eli5:
Sometimes your app reads its settings from a ConfigMap **once, when it starts up**. If you change that ConfigMap later, the already-running pods don't notice — they're still holding the old settings in memory. You need to give them a gentle nudge to restart and re-read.

`kubectl rollout restart` is that nudge. Think of a shift change at a shop: instead of locking the doors and firing everyone at once, the manager swaps staff in **one at a time** — a fresh worker clocks in, an old one clocks out, repeat — so the shop never closes.

How does it trigger a restart without actually changing anything meaningful? It stamps a tiny "restarted at `<timestamp>`" note on the recipe card (the annotation `kubectl.kubernetes.io/restartedAt`). The controller sees the card changed, so it rolls new pods — and those new pods re-read the latest ConfigMap on startup.

**Watch out for:**

- **Restart is NOT delete.** The pods are replaced **gracefully and gradually** (respecting the rolling strategy), not all killed at once. The Deployment object stays put.
- The trick is the **`restartedAt` timestamp annotation** on the pod template — that's the only thing that changes, and it's what makes it a real rollout.
- This is the **clean way to pick up a changed ConfigMap/Secret used via env vars**, since env vars don't auto-refresh in running pods.
- It rolls pods under the **current strategy** — RollingUpdate means zero downtime; Recreate means a brief gap.
- Re-running it updates the timestamp again, triggering another fresh roll each time.
questions.deepDive:
## Reload config with rollout restart — full rundown

### Mental model
Env vars (and many other inputs) are read by a container **once at startup**. Changing a ConfigMap/Secret consumed via `env`/`envFrom` does **not** update running pods. `kubectl rollout restart` forces a fresh, gradual roll so new pods read the latest config — without editing the spec meaningfully and without deleting anything.

It works by writing an annotation on the **pod template**:
```
spec.template.metadata.annotations:
  kubectl.kubernetes.io/restartedAt: "2026-11-01T12:00:00Z"
```
A template change → new ReplicaSet → rolling replacement under the current strategy.

### The command
```bash
kubectl rollout restart deployment/<name>
kubectl rollout status  deployment/<name>   # watch it finish
```
Also works on `daemonset` and `statefulset`.

### Verify the annotation
```bash
kubectl get deploy <name> \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.metadata.annotations.kubectl\.kubernetes\.io/restartedAt}'; echo
```
(The `.` in the annotation key must be escaped in JSONPath.)

### Which config sources auto-refresh vs need a restart
| Source | Mounted as volume | Used as env/envFrom |
|---|---|---|
| ConfigMap | **auto-updates** in the container (eventually, ~minute) | **needs restart** |
| Secret | auto-updates (eventually) | needs restart |
| `subPath` mount | does **not** auto-update | needs restart |

So `rollout restart` is the standard fix for env-sourced config changes and `subPath` mounts.

### restart vs other operations
| Action | Spec change? | Pods | Object kept |
|---|---|---|---|
| `rollout restart` | annotation only | **gradually** replaced (rolling) | yes |
| `delete pod` | none | killed; recreated by RS (can drop below desired briefly) | yes |
| `scale --replicas=0` then up | replicas | all down, then up | yes |
| `set image`/`set env` | real template change | rolling replace | yes |

### Rollout management commands
```bash
kubectl rollout status   deployment/<name>   # wait for completion
kubectl rollout history  deployment/<name>   # revisions
kubectl rollout undo     deployment/<name>   # roll back
kubectl rollout pause    deployment/<name>   # freeze further rollouts
kubectl rollout resume   deployment/<name>
```
Note: a `rollout restart` creates a new revision; `undo` can revert it.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Restart ≠ delete.** Pods roll gracefully per the strategy, not all-at-once; the Deployment is never removed.
- The **only** change is the `restartedAt` annotation on the template — that's the grader's evidence.
- **Env vars don't hot-reload** — editing the ConfigMap alone does nothing to running pods; restart is required.
- **Volume-mounted** ConfigMaps *do* eventually refresh in place, so a restart isn't strictly needed there (but is faster/deterministic).
- Repeated restarts each write a new timestamp → each is a genuine new rollout.
- During a RollingUpdate-strategy restart, there may transiently be old+new pods; with Recreate strategy there's a brief outage.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n deploy-learn rollout restart deployment/worker
kubectl -n deploy-learn rollout status  deployment/worker
```
